children: Titan’s Mahendra Chauhan said the company’s evolution from quartz engineering to ultra-thin mechanical watches reflects India’s growing design and manufacturing capabilities

Titan Company's journey in watchmaking illustrates how India's design and engineering capabilities have evolved from domestic manufacturing to globally competitive innovation. Mahendra Chauhan, Head of Design for Watches, Wearables, and Accessories at Titan Company, shared insights at The Future of Design Summit & Awards 2026, held in Mumbai on September 18.

During the session titled “The Design of Precision,” Chauhan recounted Titan’s design journey, which began with the development of its ultra-thin Edge quartz movement and has expanded to include newer mechanical watchmaking technologies. This session was part of the Future of Design Summit & Awards 2026 at Novotel Mumbai International Airport. Chauhan emphasised that the idea of self-reliance has been central to Titan's mission since its establishment nearly four decades ago, aiming to create a world-class watch company in India.
From 3.5 mm Quartz to 2.2 mm Mechanical

Chauhan highlighted a significant milestone for Titan in 2002 with the introduction of the Titan Edge, an ultra-thin watch measuring 3.5 mm thick. The movement was developed, engineered, and produced in India, featuring a movement thickness of approximately 1.1 mm, which Chauhan described as a remarkable engineering feat demonstrating the potential for advanced watchmaking technology in India. Over the next two decades, Titan experimented with various materials and manufacturing techniques, including carbon fiber, ceramic, titanium, and thin-ply technologies, while continually developing new forms and mechanisms.

As consumer preferences evolved, Titan began exploring the possibility of extending the Edge platform beyond quartz. However, mechanical watchmaking posed a more complex engineering challenge; a typical quartz mechanism consists of 40-50 components, while a mechanical watch has about 200-250 components. Titan addressed this challenge by building capabilities, developing skills, and investing in new machinery, eventually returning to ultra-thin watchmaking with its new Edge mechanical movement.

Launched approximately two months before the summit, this new mechanical movement measures just 2.2 mm thick. Unlike the earlier quartz movement, its gear-train structure is exposed, allowing users to appreciate the engineering, finishing, and detailing within the mechanism.

Chauhan also showcased Titan's advancements in high-end mechanical watchmaking, including its development of a tourbillon mechanism—a complex technology designed to mitigate the effects of gravity on timekeeping. Titan mastered this mechanism two years ago and incorporated it into its Jalsa watch, blending Indian engineering with traditional miniature art.

The Jalsa dial features natural stones to create vibrant colors and is hand-painted. According to Chauhan, each dial takes between 45 to 60 days to complete, with the miniature artwork crafted on a dial measuring approximately 26 mm. Additionally, Titan incorporated a sapphire magnifier connected to the minute-hand extension, allowing wearers to view intricate details of the miniature painting as the hand moves across the dial.

Chauhan remarked that Titan’s participation in the Grand Prix d’Horlogerie de Genève (GPHG) further positions Indian watchmaking alongside established international brands. Chauhan's presentation emphasised that design is not only an aesthetic discipline but also a fusion of engineering, manufacturing expertise, material innovation, and Indian craftsmanship.
